segments.title: THE LUNCH YOU CAN STILL TASTE
segments.angle: What would this idea look like if I went to its extreme? Could that open up anything interesting?

sources.text: Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Nothing twice. Never eat the same food twice. Never go to the same place twice. Never hear the same thing twice. Everything only once.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: Monotony is the enemy. Novelty is the solution.
Delayed Gratification: After a while it becomes easier with habit, routine and all. After a certain point it just becomes a positive feedback loop.
Delayed Gratification: Shallow happy is what you want now. Deep happy is what you want most.
Novelty - A Life Fully Lived: The thrill of the first. The sentimentality of the last.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Take any lunch you ate at your desk last Thursday. Same bowl, same fork, same chair. By the afternoon, could you tell anyone what was in it? So what can you still taste from last week?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nothing, I should think. Not a crumb of it. And the chipped blue bowl on this table could say the same of every supper it has ever held, in the small hours, when nobody is awake to remember them.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right. So here's what most people think about that note.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nothing twice means never repeat anything. No gym you already know. No old friend. No favourite seat. Everything new, all the time. Job done.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Job done, is it? A slogan read as a slogan would have us leaving our own beds for good. Let us read it as the rule it is.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. Read it as a rule. You're about to call it simple.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It is simple.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Simple. That's what people call a thing they never had to live.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the claim, and I promise you it is not simple at all. Monotony eats the years whole, and novelty is what keeps the days lit enough to remember.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Go on then.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So doing the same thing again and again is how a year goes missing.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I am saying repetition is an anaesthetic. You feel nothing, and then you forget you were ever in the room.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nicely put.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right, let's put it on someone. Take the extreme. A person does nothing twice for a whole year. New gym every week, a new dish every night, a different route to work every morning.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A brave soul. And a hungry one. Now tell me what they are building, midway through the year.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Muscle, obviously. Look at the new gyms.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Muscle, March?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Which gym do the muscles know? The first note told us a fit body only arrives because a man keeps going back to the same hour, the same weights, the same ache. After a certain point it just becomes a positive feedback loop. Each new gym is a stranger's weights, and nothing gets laid down.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ha. Fine.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So no body. Just a list of firsts.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A long list of firsts with no body to show for it. Tick, tick, tick, and every tick a little hollower than the one before.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ouch.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hang on, some firsts are keepers...

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Keepers, yes. The first time you eat something and think, oh, I'll be having that again. And that is the question I want the listener to answer. Is a new dish a thing to keep, or a thing to tick off? A tick is a hunt for the next box. A keeper is a thing you come back to, a little differently each time.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So a first you keep changes you. A first you tick just fills a box.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Must you always be so blunt about it? I was building a meadow, and you have walked straight across it in muddy boots.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Muddy boots. Good. Now, if you had one last day, what would you do with it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Go on, I have an answer ready, which you will find tiresome.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sit in the chair with the cold tea.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: There it is. A repeat, or a rest? Is that chair carrying you somewhere, or only keeping you still?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Oh, you are not having the chair. Back to the lunch. Does the same lunch carry you forward, or hold you still?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: It holds you still, March, and that is the test. The chair and the lunch are the same question, asked at different tables.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now put both notes on the table together. Shallow happy is what you want now. Deep happy is what you want most. Chasing novelty for its own thrill is shallow happy, a sweet at midnight with nothing behind it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And a plan with no variety just turns into a hinge that squeals every morning.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Each note sees the other's blind spot. The firsts need a future self to give them a point, and the future self needs firsts, or it goes dull.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So a first becomes a memory only if there's a body to carry it. And a repeat becomes a body only if it keeps the memory fresh.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You said it in one breath, March, which I resent, because it is exactly what I was building toward.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then show me the fork. What does someone who believes this actually do?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Think of a shelf in a kitchen. One spot is worn pale, where a hand has reached every morning for a year. Beside it sits a row of unopened things, each given a single afternoon. The believer keeps the worn spot and the row on the same shelf, and knows which one they will still be reaching for when the year turns.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A shelf I can see. Fine. That's the picture.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now the bowl on the table, March. Name what you tasted at lunch, the lunch you could not name by the afternoon. The note never asks you that, and that is precisely why it has to be asked.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You were right. Fair enough, and I'm moving on. The bill's here, and the tea's stone cold.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Must you always be so blunt, March? I was about to be magnificent. Let us give J a fresh title as well. Keeper of the Return.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'd hate that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He would hate it because it is true. Up next, Atera Matrix, where we cross the water at last.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Bring the spoon.
